units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
If there is not, the Ambassador will certainly have to be recalled. Pray point out Mrs. Cheveley to me. I should like to see her.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Let me introduce you.
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: To MRS. CHEVELEY.
My dear, Sir Robert Chiltern is dying to know you!
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: Bowing .
Every one is dying to know the brilliant Mrs. Cheveley. Our attachés at Vienna write to us about nothing else.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Thank you, Sir Robert. An acquaintance that begins with a compliment is sure to develop into a real friendship. It starts in the right manner. And I find that I know Lady Chiltern already.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Really?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes. She has just reminded me that we were at school together. I remember it perfectly now. She always got the good conduct prize. I have a distinct recollection of Lady Chiltern always getting the good conduct prize!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Smiling .
And what prizes did you get, Mrs. Cheveley?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: My prizes came a little later on in life. I don’t think any of them were for good conduct. I forget!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I am sure they were for something charming!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I don’t know that women are always rewarded for being charming. I think they are usually punished for it! Certainly, more women grow old nowadays through the faithfulness of their admirers than through anything else! At least that is the only way I can account for the terribly haggard look of most of your pretty women in London!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: What an appalling philosophy that sounds! To attempt to classify you, Mrs. Cheveley, would be an impertinence. But may I ask, at heart, are you an optimist or a pessimist? Those seem to be the only two fashionable religions left to us nowadays.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Oh, I’m neither. Optimism begins in a broad grin, and Pessimism ends with blue spectacles. Besides, they are both of them merely poses.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You prefer to be natural?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Sometimes. But it is such a very difficult pose to keep up.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: What would those modern psychological novelists, of whom we hear so much, say to such a theory as that?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Ah! the strength of women comes from the fact that psychology cannot explain us. Men can be analysed, women . . . merely adored.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You think science cannot grapple with the problem of women?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Science can never grapple with the irrational. That is why it has no future before it, in this world.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: And women represent the irrational.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Well-dressed women do.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: With a polite bow .
I fear I could hardly agree with you there. But do sit down. And now tell me, what makes you leave your brilliant Vienna for our gloomy London—or perhaps the question is indiscreet?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Questions are never indiscreet. Answers sometimes are.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Well, at any rate, may I know if it is politics or pleasure?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Politics are my only pleasure. You see nowadays it is not fashionable to flirt till one is forty, or to be romantic till one is forty-five, so we poor women who are under thirty, or say we are, have nothing open to us but politics or philanthropy. And philanthropy seems to me to have become simply the refuge of people who wish to annoy their fellow-creatures. I prefer politics. I think they are more . . . becoming!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: A political life is a noble career!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Sometimes. And sometimes it is a clever game, Sir Robert. And sometimes it is a great nuisance.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Which do you find it?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I? A combination of all three.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Drops her fan .
Picks up fan .
Allow me!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Thanks.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: But you have not told me yet what makes you honour London so suddenly. Our season is almost over.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Oh! I don’t care about the London season! It is too matrimonial. People are either hunting for husbands, or hiding from them. I wanted to meet you. It is quite true. You know what a woman’s curiosity is. Almost as great as a man’s! I wanted immensely to meet you, and . . . to ask you to do something for me.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I hope it is not a little thing, Mrs. Cheveley. I find that little things are so very difficult to do.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: After a moment’s reflection .
No, I don’t think it is quite a little thing.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I am so glad. Do tell me what it is.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Later on.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Rises .
